core_principles: The forward lunge is a fundamental movement pattern that exaggerates the lower body movements of the gait cycle.
It is an effective exercise for improving coordination, muscle balance, and performance in unilateral activities like sprinting and changing direction.
Screening an athlete's lunge pattern before applying extensive loading helps identify faulty movement strategies and reduce injury risk.
A forward lunge is executed as an elongated forward step, flexing the lead hip and knee and dorsiflexing the lead ankle while lowering the body.
common_mistakes: Executing the lunge with poor technique or faulty movement strategies before correcting movement competency.
specific_findings: The lunge is classified as 1 of 7 fundamental movement patterns (alongside squat, upper-body push, upper-body pull, bending, twisting, and gait).

The forward lunge biomechanically involves: calcaneal eversion; talar plantar flexion and adduction; tibial internal rotation; knee flexion, extension, and abduction; and hip flexion, extension, and adduction.

core_principles: The head should be straight, centrally aligned, and erect facing forward.
The thoracic spine should remain straight or slightly extended with shoulders positioned directly above the hips.
The lumbar spine must remain neutral, tall, and stable, avoiding back extension to assist hip extension.
Hips should be horizontally aligned and in line with the lead knee and ankle.
The front knee must point forward over the small toes and remain directly above the lead ankle, while the back knee is flexed.
The front foot must remain completely flat on the ground, while the back foot is positioned on the ball of the foot with toes flexed.
Ankle mobility on both the lead and trail legs is critical to maintain a balanced, biomechanically correct lunge pattern.
common_mistakes: Head positioned forward or tilted to one side.
Flexed thoracic spine due to poor or imbalanced trunk extensors.
Flexed or excessively extended lumbar spine.
Hips dropping to one side or rotating medially/laterally.
Medial or lateral movement of the knees during the lunge.
Limited ankle dorsiflexion due to stiffness in the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles.
Rolling in or out of the lead foot, turning the feet out/in, dropping the arch, or lifting the lead heel off the ground.
specific_findings: Kovacs et al. (32) and Flanagan et al. (20) found that biomechanically specious positions of the ankle and foot during squatting and lunging resulted in higher forces incurred at the knee and hip.
The ankle joint complex consists of 3 joints, namely, the ankle joint, subtalar joint, and the midtarsal joint (30,38).

core_principles: The lead knee should be positioned directly over the lead foot during a forward lunge.
The heel of the front foot must remain in contact with the ground as the center of mass moves downward.
The center of mass should move downward rather than excessively forward.
Maintain a neutral lumbar spine, avoiding both spinal flexion and excessive spinal extension.
Keep the head centered and shoulders/T-spine held down away from the ears in a neutral position.
Keep hips horizontally aligned in a 90/90 stance.
Ensure knees are aligned with the hips and feet, avoiding mediolateral movement during both eccentric and concentric phases.
common_mistakes: Mediolateral (side-to-side) movement of the lead knee during the lunge.
Allowing the center of mass to move more forward than down, causing the front heel to lift off the ground.
Excessive lumbar extension (spinal extension) to compensate for poor hip mobility.
Spinal flexion (rounding the back) during the lunge.
Allowing the knee to travel too far in front of the toes on descent.
specific_findings: Hip range of motion flexion is between 0 and 135 degrees and extension is between 0 and 15 degrees.
Allowing the center of mass to move more forward than down, lifting the front heel, increases patellofemoral shear force.

core_principles: Keep the hips parallel to the ground with no mediolateral rotation or lateral dropping.
Maintain a vertical trunk with the lumbar spine in a neutral position to minimize compressive forces.
Maintain a neutral head position with the gaze directed straight ahead to prevent excessive trunk flexion.
Screen and observe lumbar spine control during low- to moderate-intensity lunges before progressing to heavy external loads.
common_mistakes: Allowing pelvic instability and lumbar extension to compensate for limited hip mobility.
Hyperextending the lumbar spine, particularly when lifting heavier external loads.
Directing the head and gaze downward, which increases trunk flexion.
Lateral dropping or mediolateral rotation of the hips during the lunge.
specific_findings: Mean hip range of motion during a forward lunge has been reported to be 95 ± 27° of flexion.
Forces at the hip during a forward lunge are 1.25 times body weight during the downward phase and 1.31 times body weight during the upward phase.
Achieving hip mobility through pelvic instability and lumbar extension increases forces incurred by those two regions by 10% to 30%.
A 2° increase in extension from a neutral spine position increases compressive stress within the posterior annulus by an average of 16%.
Athletes hyperextend to a significant degree when lifting heavier loads at 60% and 80% of 1 repetition maximum.
A downward direction of gaze increases trunk flexion by up to 4.5° during squatting movements.

core_principles: An athlete should demonstrate several body weight forward lunges with minimal effort before progressing to external loading.
Level 3 introduces external loading using free weights, medicine balls, and other isoinertial modalities.
Level 4 focuses on the eccentric phase of the lunge pattern to demonstrate control via strength.
Levels 3 and 4 can be combined in complex loading schemes to challenge the eccentric phase under high loads.
Level 5 consists of traditional lower body plyometric drills to demonstrate movement competency at high velocities.
Do not prescribe high-velocity plyometric exercises (Level 5) before the athlete has demonstrated movement competency under high force with low velocity.
Intervention exercises like the alternate hip march and band pull with hip flexion challenge hip flexion/extension, trunk stability, and lower limb control.
To perform a forward lunge correctly, mobility must be present at the ankles and hips, and stability must be maintained at the knees and trunk.
common_mistakes: Progressing to high-velocity plyometric lunge drills (Level 5) before demonstrating competency under high force with low velocity.
Excessively loading the lunge pattern when the athlete uses compensatory movement strategies that increase injury risk.
Lacking necessary mobility at the ankles and hips, or failing to maintain stability at the knees and trunk during the lunge.
specific_findings: Level 4 focuses on the eccentric phase of the lunge pattern range of motion where the most joint forces have been recorded.
The Crazy Carpet is an 8 3 10 piece of plastic that provides friction resistance to allow a progressive lunge step distance.

core_principles: Using the body weight forward lunge as a screening tool to assess an athlete's lunge pattern.
Understanding tibiofemoral joint forces and electromyographic (EMG) activity differences between open and closed kinetic chain exercises.
